items.question: Who May Be Liable for an Accident Due to a Blind Spot?

children.text: Key Takeaways
A blind spot hides the area beside a vehicle’s pillars and behind the rear bumper that mirrors cannot cover.
The driver who failed to confirm a lane was open before moving into it usually caused the crash.
Proving negligence requires showing duty, breach, causation, and measurable damages in a blind spot accident case.
New York’s no-fault insurance law limits lawsuits for pain and suffering unless an injury meets the serious injury threshold.
Personal injury claims generally must be filed within three years, and wrongful death claims within two years.
A blind spot accident can raise an immediate question:
who is at fault in a blind spot accident

when neither driver could fully see the other coming? The driver who had the blind spot is usually deemed liable, since the duty to check for hidden vehicles falls on them. Still, this is not always the case. Fault depends on which driver violated traffic laws, and in some situations, both drivers share responsibility. For example, a driver merging into a blind spot while illegally passing on the right may bear some or all of the liability instead.
Victims of blind spot accidents have a legal right to pursue damages for economic and non-economic losses. At the
Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe
, a
Long Island car accident lawyer
can handle your case and seek compensation while you recover from the accident and your injuries.
Contact a Long Island Car Accident Lawyer Near You
Free Consultation
How Blind Spots Lead to Accidents

A blind spot causes an accident when a driver uses a lane that appears clear but is not. Mirrors and the windshield cover most of the road, but the pillars beside the seat and the space just behind the rear bumper stay hidden. A driver relying only on that visible picture merges or turns, believing no one is there, and the vehicle sitting in the blind zone cannot avoid the impact. The crash traces back to the driver who failed to confirm the lane was open before moving into it.
Several specific behaviors turn a blind spot into a collision, such as:
Changing lanes without a shoulder check to confirm the blind spot in the mirror is clear.
Lingering beside another vehicle instead of passing through its blind zone quickly.
Merging based on mirror position alone, without a direct glance.
Backing out of a space or driveway without checking behind the vehicle.
Larger vehicles, such as trucks and SUVs, have wider blind zones that hide entire cars.

On roads like the Long Island Expressway, where lanes shift constantly in heavy traffic, these moments recur often enough that blind-spot crashes occur regularly, usually resulting in sideswipe or merging
collisions
How to Prove Negligence in a Blind Spot Accident
You and your attorney must be able to prove that the other driver was behaving carelessly to file a valid
claim
. This task requires that the following circumstances be present in your case:
The driver had a duty to drive safely and observe laws.
The driver breached their duty to drive with caution.
The driver caused an accident, leading you to get hurt.
You incurred measurable
damages
Evidence needed to establish liability may include vehicle photos, surveillance video, the crash report, traffic citations, medical records, and
eyewitness
and expert testimony.
How New York’s No-Fault Insurance Laws Impact Blind Spot Accidents
New York operates under a no-fault insurance system,
which changes how compensation is determined after a blind-spot collision. Under
New York Insurance Law Section 5104

, an injured driver generally cannot sue another driver for pain and suffering unless the injury meets the state’s serious injury threshold. This rule applies to blind-spot accidents the same as any other crash, so many victims first recover medical costs and lost wages through their own no-fault benefits, regardless of who caused the collision.

Fault still matters once an injury meets that threshold. The driver whose blind-spot negligence caused the crash can then be held liable for pain and suffering and other losses that no-fault coverage does not cover. Determining
who is at fault in a blind spot accident
requires more than a police report, and an attorney can review medical records and crash details before assuming a claim is limited to basic benefits.
What Types of Damages Will an Auto Accident Settlement Cover?
Damages are a form of monetary compensation that a victim of an accident can pursue in a claim or lawsuit. The two main types of damages are economic and non-economic damages.
Economic damages are the most common and easily identifiable types of compensation. Alternatively, non-economic damages cannot be readily tied to a dollar amount.
Past and Future Medical Costs

If you provide copies of medical bills, the liable party may reimburse you for these costs. If you expect to incur future expenses for more treatments, therapies, surgeries, and prescriptions, you could claim compensation for these expenses, as well.
Lost Wages and Potential Earnings
If accident-related injuries left you unfit to work, you could qualify to recover lost income. If you cannot return to work in the future, these lost potential earnings may also be recoverable.
Accident-Related Out of Pocket Expenses
Out-of-pocket costs you can recoup may include travel expenses and vehicle repair and replacement costs.
If your injury has made childcare or housekeeping challenging or unattainable, you may be awarded compensation for daycare, cleaning help, and other household assistance.
Pain and Suffering
Pain and suffering refers to physical pain and discomfort experienced during and after an accident.
Loss of Consortium

Loss of consortium is a legal term that refers to losing a significant other’s or spouse’s physical companionship. If you or a passenger was injured and the accident affected a relationship(s), you might be qualified to receive these damages.
Loss of Enjoyment of Life

An auto accident can entirely alter a person’s life, and you may discover your injuries make it more challenging to engage in activities once enjoyed or go about life as you once did. If you can no longer participate in your normal daily activities, you may also be entitled to collect reimbursement for these losses.
Wrongful Death Damages
Tragically, car accident victims may lose their lives to related injuries. If that was the case for your loved one, you could pursue wrongful death damages, including:
Funeral and burial expenses
Final medical bills
Loss of household services
How Long You Have to Take Legal Action After a Blind Spot Accident
If filing a lawsuit is the most appropriate legal route for you, you must be aware of the time limits the state enforces:
Personal injury:
CVP § 214
affirms that you generally have three years to file.
Wrongful death:
says that you typically have two years to file.
Waiting too long to submit your case may prompt the state to refuse to hear it, leaving you with few options for compensation.
Safety Tips to Avoid Blind Spots
Preventing a blind spot crash starts with defensive habits every driver can practice, including:
Check mirrors and glance over your shoulder before every lane change.
Signal early to give nearby drivers time to react.
Pause before merging to confirm no vehicle is hidden in the blind zone.
Avoid lingering beside a truck or SUV, since larger vehicles carry wider blind spots.
Pass through another vehicle’s blind zone quickly rather than riding alongside it.
Even careful drivers cannot control how attentive others are on the road. When a collision occurs despite these precautions,
who
is
at
fault
in
a
blind-spot accident
still needs a clear legal answer grounded in evidence, not assumptions made at the scene.

who is at fault in a blind spot accident
. At the
Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe

items.question: Do I Have a Case if I Didn’t Visit the Doctor After My Car Accident?

children.text: Key Takeaways
Adrenaline after a car accident can mask concussions and internal bleeding for hours.
Crashes involving two or more vehicles cause more injuries than single-vehicle wrecks, despite fewer fatalities.
Bleeding that will not stop, chest pain, or loss of consciousness requires immediate emergency care.
Soreness without emergency symptoms still warrants a same-day or next-day medical evaluation.
Very low-speed impacts with no visible injury may only need a primary doctor follow-up.

A crash on the Long Island Expressway can end in seconds, but the physical toll often unfolds over the hours that follow. Adrenaline floods the body after any collision and can mask pain a person would otherwise notice right away. This is why so many crash victims ask themselves, “
Should I go to the hospital after a car accident

?” even when they feel fine at the scene. The answer is that shock and adrenaline can hide serious injuries such as a concussion or internal bleeding, and prompt evaluation creates the medical record that protects a crash victim’s health and any future injury claim.
At
the Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe,
we guide families through these first decisions, and speaking with a
Long Island car accident lawyer
early can help protect a person’s health and their case.
How Common Are Injuries After a Car Accident?
Collisions between two or more cars cause the vast majority of crash injuries nationwide. Multi-car wrecks account for less than half of all motor vehicle fatalities, according to the
National Safety Council
; still, this same crash type represents 79 percent of injuries and 74 percent of injury
crashes
reported nationwide.
Single-car wrecks involving fixed objects, pedestrians, or rollovers cause a larger share of
fatalities relative to their frequency
, but multi-car collisions remain the most common source of the aches, strains, and hidden trauma that bring drivers to urgent care or the emergency room.
Warning Signs That You Should Go to the Hospital After a Car Accident
Recognizing whether someone needs emergency room care after a car accident can be difficult in the disorienting minutes following a crash. According to
MedlinePlus
, bleeding that will not stop, breathing difficulty, sudden confusion,
chest pain
lasting two minutes or longer, and fainting or loss of consciousness are all signs of a medical emergency.
A driver or
passenger
who experiences any of the following after a crash should head straight to an emergency room or call for emergency services:
Loss of consciousness
Trouble breathing or severe chest pain
Bleeding that will not stop
Sudden headaches, dizziness, confusion, or vision changes
Numbness or an inability to move the
neck
or limbs
Abdominal pain or swelling that could point to internal bleeding
Waiting on these symptoms can allow a hidden injury to worsen while the opportunity to document it fades.
When to Seek Urgent or Next-Day Care

For many drivers, whether to go to the hospital after a car accident depends more on timing than on an obvious injury. A driver with no emergency symptoms who still feels sore, stiff, or generally off should visit a local urgent care clinic or their primary doctor for a same-day or next-day examination.
This prompt visit still generates documentation that may be needed later for an insurance claim or legal case, even without ambulance transport.
Whiplash
and
soft-tissue

strains usually surface hours after the initial jolt of a crash, sometimes the next morning, once the initial adrenaline fades. Waiting several days gives insurers the opportunity to argue the injury came from something else entirely, while a same-day visit closes that gap.
Reasons You Might Not Need to Visit an Emergency Room
Not every fender-bender calls for a trip to the emergency room. Understanding
whether someone should go to the hospital

after a car accident usually means weighing recovery time against the value of a documented exam. A driver who feels no pain, shows no visible injury, and was involved in a very low-speed impact may reasonably choose a follow-up visit with a primary care doctor instead of hours in an ER waiting room.

Emergency departments treat life-threatening conditions first, so minor bumps and bruises are often triaged behind more urgent cases. Urgent care or a scheduled doctor visit can still produce the medical record needed later, without that same wait.

items.question: Can You Sue Someone For a Car Accident?

children.text: Key Takeaways
Injured people in New York may sue an at-fault driver after a car accident when the case meets the requirements established under New York law.
New York’s no-fault law limits lawsuits unless an injury meets the serious injury threshold.
As of May 2026, New York removed the 90/180-day category from its serious injury definition.
Insurance settlement offers may not fully reflect the true value of an injury claim.
Damages available in a lawsuit may include medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering.
A car accident in Queens can turn a routine drive into a life-altering event within seconds. Many ask,
can you sue someone for a car accident
once insurance talks stall or fall short? The answer is often yes, and knowing when that path makes sense can mean the difference between a fair recovery and years of financial strain.
At the
Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe – Queens Personal Injury Lawyers,
we help injured Queens residents pursue accountability after a crash, and a
Queens car accident lawyer
on our team can help explain how New York law applies to your specific circumstances.
Contact a Queens Car Accident Attorney Near You
Free Consultation
Reasons To Sue Another Driver

Most car accident claims in Queens resolve through an insurance payout, but several circumstances push injured drivers toward suing another driver instead. When a driver’s carelessness, such as distracted or reckless driving, causes a crash, the injured party may have grounds for legal action. New York law requires proof of duty, breach, and the resulting injury.

Some collisions raise liability questions beyond driver error. A defective vehicle part, a poorly maintained road, or a commercial driver acting outside company policy can each provide grounds for legal action beyond a standard insurance claim. These situations usually surprise accident victims, especially when they initially assumed their case would end quietly with a settlement check.
The Role of No-Fault Laws in New York

New York operates under a no-fault insurance system, unlike many other states. Injured drivers first turn to their own insurance policy for medical expenses and lost income, regardless of who caused the crash. This system speeds up compensation, but it limits the right to sue for pain and suffering unless the injury meets a specific legal threshold under
New York Insurance Law § 5104

That threshold is known as a serious injury, a term with a legal definition rather than a general description of severity. Fractures, significant disfigurement, and permanent loss or limitation of a body part or system are among the qualifying categories. As of May 2026, New York has removed the temporary 90/180-day category, so a short-term limitation on daily activities alone no longer meets the threshold.

Once an injury satisfies New York’s legal requirements for a lawsuit, an injured person may pursue damages beyond those available through no-fault benefits, including pain and suffering where permitted by law.
Insurance Negotiations May Not Cover Your Damages
Adjusters are trained to close claims quickly, which often leaves victims with an offer that does not reflect the true cost of their injuries. Whether
you can sue someone for a car accident

often depends on how these negotiations unfold, not on the crash itself. Medical bills that keep growing, income lost during recovery, and long-term therapy needs usually exceed what a first settlement offer covers.
Because of this, consider speaking with a
Queens car accident lawyer
before accepting any settlement or signing paperwork from an insurance company. Knowing
what to expect when filing an accident claim

in New York helps set realistic expectations before negotiations begin. An early conversation with our team can clarify whether an offer reflects the full value of a claim or whether pursuing a lawsuit against the negligent driver would better protect a client’s financial future.
Compensation That Could Be Available to You
When a car accident lawsuit moves forward in Queens, the damages available often go beyond
basic economic loss
under no-fault insurance, falling into two categories: measurable financial losses and the harder-to-quantify toll an injury takes on daily life.
Common categories may include:
Medical Expenses: Hospital bills, surgeries, and ongoing treatment tied to the crash.
Lost Wages: Income missed during recovery, including reduced future earning capacity.
Property Damage: Repair or replacement costs for a damaged vehicle.
Pain and Suffering: Physical pain and emotional distress caused by the injury.
Loss of Enjoyment: Reduced ability to participate in hobbies or daily activities.
Every case looks different, and whether
you can sue someone for a car accident
comes down to the severity of the injury, the strength of the evidence, and how the damages can be documented.

items.question: Common Causes of Truck Accidents in New York

children.text: Key Takeaways
Driver fatigue from Hours-of-Service violations is one of the most common and preventable causes of truck crashes in New York.
Federal regulations require commercial truck drivers to take mandatory rest periods before returning to the road.
Distracted driving in commercial vehicles reduces reaction time and increases crash severity in New York’s stop-and-go traffic.
Improperly loaded cargo shifts during transit, altering a truck’s center of gravity and raising rollover risk on Long Island roads.
Tractor-trailers have
blind spots
on all four sides, making improper mirror checks a leading cause of sideswipe collisions.

Every year, thousands of people across New York are seriously injured in collisions involving commercial trucks. Most of these crashes were preventable, which raises a question that families and survivors ask constantly:
What are the common causes of truck accidents?

Driver fatigue, distracted driving, speeding, and poor vehicle maintenance top the list across New York, while blind-spot negligence and improper cargo loading drive additional crashes along the state’s busiest commercial corridors and densely packed urban streets.

On Long Island, where the Long Island Expressway and Sunrise Highway carry heavy freight traffic daily, the consequences can be devastating. Victims hurt in these collisions deserve legal representation. At
Law Office of Cohen & Jaffe – Long Island Personal Injury Lawyers
, our
Long Island truck accident lawyer
team can help you navigate the legal process after a serious collision.
Contact a Long Island Truck Accident Lawyer Near You
Free Consultation
Frequent Factors Contributing to Truck Accidents in NY
Drivers, carriers, and loading crews each contribute to
what are common causes of truck accidents

on New York roads. Commercial trucks operate under federal regulations and physical limitations that passenger drivers never face. When any one of these factors is mismanaged on Long Island’s congested roads, the results can be catastrophic. The most common contributing factors may include:
Driver Fatigue
Tight delivery schedules often push drivers to violate federal Hours-of-Service rules. Under
49 C.F.R. Part 395

, a driver may not operate a commercial motor vehicle without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty and may not drive beyond a 14-hour window after coming on duty. Exhausted drivers suffer slower reaction times, impaired judgment, and a sharply elevated risk of microsleep.
Distracted Driving
Using a GPS device, eating, or texting prevents drivers from reacting to the sudden stops that define New York traffic. According to the recent data from the
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration

, distracted driving claimed 3,208 lives in previous years and injured more than 315,000 others. For operators of vehicles weighing up to 80,000 pounds, even a momentary lapse carries fatal consequences.
Speeding and Reckless Driving

Commercial trucks require far more distance to brake safely than passenger vehicles. Speeding, tailgating, and the “squeeze play,” where a truck swings wide to complete a right turn and cuts off surrounding traffic, are recurring patterns in Long Island intersection and merge-zone crashes.
Poor Vehicle Maintenance

Defective brakes, worn tires, and broken lighting systems can cause a driver to lose control without warning. Federal regulations require carriers to perform regular inspections on every vehicle in their fleet. Deferred maintenance on Long Island routes can lead to direct collisions.
Improper Loading

Cargo that is unevenly distributed or left unsecured moves during transit. This alters the truck’s center of gravity, which can trigger rollovers on the curved highway interchanges connecting Long Island’s major expressways.
Blind Spots
Tractor-trailers carry massive blind spots, known as “No-Zones,” on all four sides. The
FMCSA

advises drivers to check mirrors every 8 to 10 seconds and scan 15 seconds ahead. Failing to follow the protocol before merging on multi-lane New York highways frequently results in passenger vehicles being sideswiped.
Weather Factors

Rain, snow, and ice demand deliberate adjustments to speed and following distance. Failure to adapt makes commercial trucks prone to jackknifing or skidding, especially on elevated roadways and bridge approaches where surface temperatures drop fastest.
Quick Tips to Prevent Truck Crashes in New York
A few habits can reduce Long Island drivers’ exposure to these collisions, including:
Stay Out of No-Zones: If the driver cannot see you in their mirrors, they cannot account for your position.
Allow Extra Following Distance: Trucks need much more space to stop. Staying back gives both drivers time to react.
Pass Decisively: Clear the vehicle quickly rather than lingering in a blind spot.
Anticipate Wide Turns: Stay well behind the rear axle when a truck signals right at an intersection.

items.question: Is New York a No-Fault State?

children.text: Key Takeaways
New York is a no-fault state requiring drivers to file injury claims with their own insurer first.
Personal Injury Protection covers medical bills and a portion of lost wages after any accident.
Written notice of a no-fault claim must be filed within 30 calendar days of the accident.
Serious injuries meeting New York’s legal threshold allow victims to sue the at-fault driver directly.
No-fault benefits can be denied if the driver was intoxicated, impaired, or committing a felony.
New York roads carry millions of drivers every day, and accidents happen without warning. A question many injured drivers ask immediately after a crash is:
Is New York a no-fault state?

The answer is yes. New York operates under a no-fault car insurance system, which means injured drivers turn to their own insurer first for medical costs and lost wages, regardless of who was at fault in the crash. Personal injury protection coverage is required by law, and a written claim must reach the insurer within 30 days of the accident.
At the
Law Office of Cohen & Jaffe – Long Island Personal Injury Lawyers
, our
car
accident attorneys in Long Island
can help you understand how this system shapes your recovery and your options after a collision.
Key Elements of New York No-Fault Law
New York’s no-fault framework rests on four pillars that govern every car accident claim in the state.
PIP Coverage
Personal Injury Protection is mandatory for every registered vehicle in New York. Under
New York Insurance Law § 5103

, every owner’s liability policy must provide first-party benefits covering medical treatment, a portion of lost wages, and other necessary expenses resulting from an accident, regardless of which driver caused it.
Threshold to Sue
No-fault covers immediate costs but not pain and suffering. To pursue those damages, an injury must meet the state’s
serious injury threshold

. Qualifying conditions include significant disfigurement, bone fracture, permanent loss or limitation of a body organ, member, function, or system, or significant limitation of use of a body function or system.
Deadline
Time matters under the no-fault law. According to the
New York Department of Financial Services

, injured individuals must file a written notice of claim with the no-fault insurer as soon as reasonably practicable, but no later than 30 calendar days after the accident. Missing that window can result in a denial of benefits regardless of injury severity.
Exclusions
No-fault benefits are not guaranteed in every situation. Coverage may be denied when the injured driver was intoxicated, impaired by drugs, committing a felony, or intentionally caused the accident.
Who Is Covered by No-Fault Benefits in New York After an Accident?

No-fault benefits extend beyond the vehicle owner; passengers injured in a covered vehicle are generally entitled to first-party benefits, as are pedestrians struck by a registered New York vehicle. The coverage follows the accident rather than the individual’s fault in causing it. The idea behind New York’s no-fault system is straightforward: injured people should have access to medical coverage quickly instead of waiting months or years for liability disputes to play out. That principle sits at the core of
New York’s no-fault insurance system
What’s Not Covered?

No-fault has clear limits. Property damage to your vehicle and personal belongings is not covered by PIP and must be addressed through a separate claim. Most significantly, non-economic damages such as pain and suffering, emotional distress, and loss of enjoyment of life are not recoverable under no-fault. Those categories only become available when an injury meets New York’s serious injury threshold, which requires conditions such as permanent loss of a body organ, member, function, or system, significant disfigurement, or significant limitation of use of a body function or system.
When Can You Step Outside No-Fault?

When injuries qualify as serious, state law permits an injured person to bring a claim directly against the at-fault driver. This opens the door to compensation for pain and suffering, permanent disability, and long-term income loss beyond PIP limits. New York applies a
comparative negligence rule
, meaning damages are reduced in proportion to the claimant’s share of fault. Recent changes to New York law may limit the recovery of certain
non-economic damages
when an injured person is found more at fault than the defendant.
This matters in complex cases where liability is disputed, a reality many drivers face when asking:
Is New York a no-fault state?
Acting quickly protects evidence and your right to pursue the full value of your claim.

Steps to File a Car Accident Claim in New York

New York follows a no-fault insurance system, meaning your Personal Injury Protection (PIP) coverage pays for initial medical expenses and a portion of lost wages regardless of who caused the collision.
Filing a
car accident claim

Report the Crash to the DMV: Under Section 605 of the
New York State Vehicle and Traffic Law
, drivers must file a report if someone is injured or killed, property damage exceeds $1,000, or an e-bike is involved. Failing to file may result in a suspended license.
Seek Medical Attention: Even when injuries feel minor, a prompt evaluation creates a documented record linking your condition to the accident.

Tips for a Successful Car Accident Claim in NY

Also, avoid posting about the accident on social media, as photographs and comments can surface in litigation and contradict injury claims. Statute of Limitations for Car Accident Claims in New York

items.question: Can I Sue the Driver of the Vehicle If I Am a Passenger in a Car Accident in New York?

children.text: Key Takeaways
Passengers injured in a New York car accident can pursue compensation from one or more at-fault drivers.
New York’s no-fault system requires passengers to first file a PIP claim before pursuing a lawsuit.
To sue for pain and suffering, a passenger’s injuries must meet New York’s serious injury threshold.
New York’s pure comparative fault rule allows recovery even when a driver is only partially at fault.
A car accident attorney can identify all liable parties and pursue every available avenue for compensation.
When
I was a passenger in a car accident, who do I sue

is one of the first questions that comes to mind after a crash. Every motorist has a duty of care to keep others safe from an unreasonable risk of harm, and negligent drivers can be held financially responsible when their actions cause injuries to others. Depending on the circumstances, it may be possible to sue the at-fault driver of the vehicle you were riding in, the driver of another vehicle that struck your car, or both.
At
Law Office of Cohen & Jaffe
our
car accident attorney in Long Island
can help injured passengers identify every available avenue to pursue the compensation they deserve under the law.
Understanding Passenger Rights in New York Car Accidents

New York law treats passengers as third parties with distinct rights. Since they are not typically involved in the cause of the accident, passengers can pursue compensation from one or more drivers involved, including:
The driver of the vehicle they were riding in.
Drivers of other vehicles were involved in the crash.
Vehicle owners or entities responsible for the operation of any involved vehicle.
These rights are reinforced by New York’s no-fault benefits structure, which allows passengers to claim personal injury protection (PIP) benefits regardless of fault. PIP typically covers:
Medical expenses
Lost earnings equal to 80% of lost income, up to $2,000 per month for up to three years
Necessary and reasonable expenses (up to $25/day for up to 1 year).
However, if PIP benefits don’t cover the full extent of injuries, and the passenger’s harm qualifies as “
serious

” under New York law, they can sue to recover additional damages such as pain and suffering. This becomes especially important when evaluating whether a passenger can pursue claims against multiple drivers whose negligence contributed to the accident.
When Can a Passenger Sue a Non-at-Fault Driver?

A passenger generally cannot recover damages from a driver who bears no responsibility for the accident. However, some collisions involve multiple drivers whose actions contributed to the crash. In these situations, under New York’s
comparative negligence
rule, a passenger may pursue compensation from each party whose negligence contributed to the accident.
Common scenarios may include:
Comparative Negligence Applies: New York follows a pure comparative fault rule, which allows injured parties to recover damages when more than one driver contributed to the collision.

Policy Limits Are Insufficient: If one driver’s insurance coverage is insufficient to fully compensate the injured passenger, additional claims may be available against other parties whose negligence contributed to the crash.

Negligent Behavior Still Contributed: A driver may share responsibility for an accident if their actions helped cause the collision, such as speeding, driving while distracted, following too closely, or failing to react appropriately to roadway conditions.
Important New York Legal Thresholds
As a passenger injured in a car accident on Long Island, two key legal thresholds will determine how your claim proceeds under New York law.
No-Fault Insurance: Regardless of who was at fault, you will first file a no-fault insurance claim to cover medical expenses and lost wages.
“Serious Injury” Threshold: To file a lawsuit against another driver, your injuries must meet the legal definition of “serious” under
Insurance Law § 5104
, including significant disfigurement, bone fractures, permanent limitation of use of a body organ or member, or significant limitation of use of a body system.
It is recommended to consult a
Long Island car accident attorney
to identify the strategy and all available insurance coverage.
What to Do After a Car Accident as a Passenger
To protect your right to sue, passengers should take the following steps:
Seek medical treatment immediately, even if injuries seem minor.
Report the accident to the insurance carrier within 30 days to access no-fault benefits.
Document all injuries and expenses with medical records and receipts.
Request copies of the police report and witness statements.
Consult with a car accident attorney who is familiar with the courts and accident laws.
New York Motorists Must Drive With Care
Under
Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1146

, every New York motorist has a duty of care to others on the road, including passengers in other vehicles. Motorists who fail to meet this standard and cause a collision can face criminal penalties and financial liability for the injuries they cause.
Some dangerous behaviors that could have caused your accident include:
A driver being intoxicated or under the influence of drugs
Tailgating
Speeding
Changing lanes erratically
Making improper turns
Driving on parts of the road where vehicles are not permitted
Disobeying traffic safety signals, such as stop signs and red lights

Your accident may have also been the result of distracted driving. These practices can be especially dangerous on the busy streets of New York, where taking your eyes off the road for even a second could cause an accident. According to the recent data from the
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
, distracted driving claimed 3,208 lives in previous years.
To recover compensation, you will need to determine why the accident occurred. You may choose to work with a
Long Island Personal Injury Lawyer
to complete this task.
Liability for Your New York Car Accident
Depending on the circumstances of your accident, you may be able to hold more than one party accountable for your losses.
In addition to the at-fault motorist, you may be able to recover compensation from:
The employer of the at-fault driver, if they were operating a commercial vehicle
A vehicle or parts manufacturer whose product did not function properly
A mechanic whose subpar work is tied to the accident
A municipality responsible for a roadway’s maintenance
A lawyer can help identify every liable party and determine whether you can sue the driver of a vehicle as a passenger in a New York car accident.
How a Lawyer May Assist You

Being injured or losing a loved one in a car accident can take a physical, emotional, and financial toll. However, having a lawyer to assist with your legal matters following an accident can work to relieve your stress. While your lawyer’s primary goal is to obtain any compensation that you are entitled to, they aim to do more than that.

items.question: A Guide to Getting a Car Accident Police Report in New York

children.text: Key Takeaways
NY law requires a report when a crash causes injury or over $1,000 property damage.
If police do not respond, drivers must file MV-104 with DMV within 10 days.
Accident reports are used by insurers and DMV to determine liability.
NYC reports become available online about 14 days after the crash.
Precinct keeps reports for 30 days before sending them to the DMV.
Getting an
NYC accident report

after a crash is one of the most important steps toward protecting your legal rights. This document records the official facts of the collision, identifies all parties involved, and plays a central role in determining fault for any injury or property damage claim. New York state law requires a report to be filed whenever a crash results in injury or more than $1,000 in property damage.
At
Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe
, a
car accident lawyer in Long Island
helps injured drivers navigate this process so no critical detail gets overlooked.
Contact a Long Island Car Accident Lawyer Near You
Free Consultation
How to Obtain a Car Accident Police Report in New York
New York state law requires police to file a report when responding to an accident causing over $1,000 in damage or injury to any parties involved. In cases where the
police do not respond
to such an accident, the drivers involved must file an accident report with the New York Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV). The official title for this report is the
Report of Motor Vehicle Accident (MV-104)
. The purpose of the MV-104 is to establish the facts that led up to the accident.
Securing a New York car accident police report can be accomplished through several accessible methods:
Online: For collisions within New York City, the
NYPD online portal

provides digital access to request reports. The NY DMV website offers another online ordering option, though electronically submitted reports from NYC boroughs generally become available approximately 14 days following the crash, while reports from other areas may need additional processing time. Online requests often prove fastest after reports become available.

In Person: Victims can appear at the precinct responding to the accident, bringing the report number if available, or providing details like the date, time, location, and vehicle information. If you don’t know the specific precinct, the NYPD website includes a precinct finder tool based on the accident location.
By Mail: Those preferring mail requests can send the completed form to the Traffic Safety Officer at the relevant precinct.

The DMV and the drivers’ insurance companies will use the facts contained in the report to determine liability for the accident. This will begin the claims process. If you’re a driver in New York, you should know how to obtain a copy of this report. However, if you want to file a claim in New York for a vehicle accident, you
don’t necessarily need a police report
to move forward.
Online Crash Report Sales Portal: Quick Guide
The Online Crash Report Sales Portal is the fastest way to request an
NYC accident report
without visiting a precinct. According to the
New York DMV

, there are two paths into the portal depending on whether a driver already holds an NY.gov ID. Those with an existing account click “Order Crash Reports Online,” sign in with their credentials, and complete a shared secrets setup before reaching the order screen. Drivers without an account can create an NY.gov ID before proceeding through the same steps.

Once inside the portal, the system requests basic details such as the date of the crash, location, and names of involved parties. Accurate information helps locate the correct report quickly. Payment follows through a secure checkout, and digital copies typically arrive soon after confirmation.

Many drivers encounter delays due to minor errors, such as incorrect dates or misspelled names. Verifying those details before submitting avoids unnecessary delays. A properly obtained report supports a car accident claim and provides clarity during the early stages of a legal case.
What Kind of Information Is in the Accident Report?
The accident report will contain valuable information about the accident. The type of information requested in an accident report includes, but is not limited to, the following:
Date of the accident
Time of the accident
Location of the accident
Make and model year of vehicles involved
License plate numbers of vehicles involved
Driver’s license numbers for all drivers involved
Name of any passenger(s) involved in the accident
Contact information for driver(s), passenger(s), and witness(es)
Insurance policy information for all drivers involved
General weather conditions (e.g., wet, snowy, raining, sunny, dusk) at the time of the accident
Summary of any injuries to drivers, passengers, cyclists, or pedestrians involved
Any moving violations or other citations issued by police
Description of any damage to vehicles or property
Sketches or drawings that describe the accident (e.g., direction of vehicles before and after the accident)

If the police respond to the accident, they will file the report automatically. However, if they do not, New York law requires the drivers involved to file form MV-104 with the DMV no later than 10 days after the accident. The MV-104 will also become part of the official records for each driver involved in the accident. Every detail counts, so provide as much information as possible.
Why do I Need a Copy of My Accident Report?
If the police didn’t respond to your accident and issue a citation at the scene, it’s possible that one or more of the other drivers involved may contest liability.

That’s why your insurance company (and that of the other driver) will use the accident report to assess which driver was more at fault in causing the accident. This is just part of why it is so important to contact an experienced attorney immediately after an accident.
How do I Get a Copy of My Accident Report

If the police responded to your accident, you should get a copy of the report from the police station for the precinct where the accident happened. Generally, the report will be available no later than 30 days after the accident. If, however, the police did not respond and you submitted an accident report yourself, you will need to complete the
Request for Copy of Collision Record Form

You can fill this form out online, but remember to make two copies. Once you have completed both copies, you can mail them to the police precinct where the accident occurred or drop them off in person at the precinct. The NYPD also has an
online service
where you can request a copy of your accident report.

However, the report may not be available until at least seven business days after the accident. The precinct will retain copies of the accident report for 30 days after the accident, after which they are forwarded to the New York State Commissioner of Motor Vehicles. If you don’t request your accident report from the precinct within this 30-day period, you must get your accident report directly from the DMV.
Do You Need a Lawyer to Get a Report?

No, a lawyer is not required to obtain a crash report, but legal guidance can make the process more effective. Attorneys review reports for accuracy, identify missing details, and connect the information to a broader legal strategy. Small inconsistencies can affect liability arguments, especially in cases involving multiple drivers or injuries. Having counsel manage follow-ups when agencies delay responses keeps the case moving while clients focus on recovery.

NYC accident report
is one of the important pieces of information you can have. Obtaining it while dealing with injuries and property damage can be overwhelming. Our team at

items.question: What is the Definition of a Motor Vehicle Accident?

children.text: Key Takeaways
Motor vehicle accident means an unplanned event where a vehicle strikes another vehicle, a person, or an object.
Accidents result from human error, vehicle malfunction, or environmental conditions.
Head-on collisions occur when the front of one vehicle strikes the front of another.
A crash includes three impacts: vehicle impact, occupant impact, and internal organ movement.
In New York, injured parties may seek compensation for losses caused by another’s negligent driving.

A car accident, also called a traffic collision, is an unplanned event in which a motor vehicle strikes another vehicle, a pedestrian, an animal, or a stationary object. These incidents frequently result from human error, such as distracted driving, speeding, or failure to yield, as well as environmental factors like poor road conditions or reduced visibility, and they can lead to serious injuries, fatalities, and significant property damage
For drivers across Long Island, the question:
what is a car accident?

and what legal consequences follow? Often arises in the immediate aftermath of a collision. Understanding the definition is the foundation for determining liability, pursuing compensation, and protecting your rights under New York law.
At
Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe
our
Long Island car accident lawyers
helps injured drivers and families move forward after a crash with clear legal guidance from the beginning.
Understanding Motor Vehicle Accidents
Motor vehicle accidents are a leading cause of injury and death worldwide. According to the
World Health Organization

, approximately 1.19 million people are killed in road traffic crashes every year, with between 20 and 50 million more sustaining non-fatal injuries, many of which result in lasting disability. In the United States, the
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
recorded 40,901 fatalities in motor vehicle traffic crashes in its most recent reporting period, a 4.3 percent decrease from the previous year.

These incidents can stem from a range of factors, including human error, vehicle malfunction, and environmental conditions. Understanding what contributes to motor vehicle accidents is essential for preventing them and reducing the likelihood of serious injury or death.
Head-on Collisions
Head-on collisions
are some of the most dangerous types of car accidents. This type of accident, which is also known as a front-end collision, occurs when the front of one vehicle strikes the front of another.

Head-on collisions make up a large portion of fatal car accidents, as the force generated by two fast-moving cars striking each other while traveling in opposite directions can be extreme. Common motor vehicle accident injuries from head-on collisions include severe trauma to the head, neck, and spine, as well as psychological impacts that require prompt medical evaluation and integrated care plans.
Side-Impact Collisions

Side-impact collisions come in two different forms: T-bone and broadside accidents. A T-bone accident occurs when the front of a motor vehicle strikes the side of another car. Broadside collisions happen when the sides of two cars collide.
Rear-end Collisions
The most common type of car accident, a rear-end collision, involves one driver colliding with the back-end of another. These accidents are commonly linked to a neck injury known as whiplash.
Rollover Accidents

Rollover accidents occur when a driver loses control of their car and rolls end-over-end. Rollover accidents can occur after a collision with another vehicle, but they are frequently one-car accidents.
Single-vehicle Accidents

Single-vehicle accidents involve a car striking a stationary object such as a tree, pole, or barrier. New York crash reports require drivers to identify fixed objects involved in a collision, including utility poles, guardrails, or buildings, according to the
New York Department of Motor Vehicles
The Three Collisions

A motor vehicle crash includes three distinct impacts: the vehicle hitting an object, occupants striking the vehicle interior, and internal organs moving within the body. Each stage contributes to injury severity, which can become a key factor when evaluating damages after a serious car crash.
Causes of Motor Vehicle Accidents
There are several causes of motor vehicle accidents, including:
Distracted Driving:

Distracted driving is a leading cause of motor vehicle accidents. This can include texting, talking on the phone, eating, or engaging in any other activity that takes a driver’s attention away from the road.
Speeding: Speeding
is a major contributor to motor vehicle accidents. Excessive speed can increase the risk of losing control of a vehicle, and it can also increase the severity of injuries in the event of a crash.
Drunk Driving:
Drunk driving is a serious offense that can have devastating consequences.
Alcohol impairs a driver’s ability to react quickly
and make sound judgments, increasing the risk of a motor vehicle accident.
Reckless Driving:

Reckless driving includes behaviors such as tailgating, weaving in and out of lanes, and running red lights. These behaviors can increase the risk of a motor vehicle accident and put other drivers and pedestrians at risk.
Vehicle Malfunction:
Vehicle malfunction can also contribute to motor vehicle accidents. This can include issues with brakes, tires, or other critical systems.
Environmental Conditions:
Environmental conditions such as rain, snow, or fog can increase the risk of a motor vehicle accident. Drivers should exercise caution and adjust their driving habits accordingly.
Common Car Accident-Related Injuries

A car accident could result in devastating physical injuries. Some accidents are more severe than others, but even seemingly minor collisions could lead to long-term disabilities or chronic pain. Motor vehicle accidents can also result in pedestrian injuries, which are often severe. Some common accident-related injuries include:
Cuts and bruises
Broken bones
Internal bleeding
Severe burns
Head trauma
Cracked ribs
Paralysis
Amputation
Spinal cord damage
Sprains and strains

The cost of recovering from these injuries can be extensive, both in terms of time and money. While a personal injury lawsuit cannot speed up your physical recovery, it could provide you with the financial compensation needed to pay for your treatment. Consulting with a personal injury lawyer or personal injury lawyers is crucial for filing personal injury claims after sustaining injuries in a car accident to ensure all necessary documents are filed within the required timeframe for compensation.
After a Car Accident
If you are involved in a motor vehicle accident, there are several steps you should take to ensure your safety and protect your rights. These include:
Seek Medical Attention

: If you are injured, seek medical attention immediately. Even if you do not appear to be injured, it is still important to see a doctor as soon as possible. Some injuries may not be immediately apparent, and a medical professional can help diagnose and treat any potential issues.
Call the Police
: Call the police and report the accident. This will help create a record of the incident and can be useful in any future legal proceedings.
Gather Evidence
: Gather as much evidence as possible from the scene of the accident. This can include photos of the vehicles and any damage, witness statements, and any other relevant information.
Notify Your Insurance Company
: Notify your insurance company as soon as possible. They can help guide you through the process of filing a claim and can provide you with any necessary support.
Consult with a Personal Injury Lawyer

: If you are injured in a motor vehicle accident, it may be helpful to consult with a personal injury lawyer. They can help you navigate the legal process and ensure that you receive any compensation you are entitled to.
By understanding the causes of motor vehicle accidents and taking the necessary steps after an accident, you can help reduce the risk of injury or death and protect your rights.
The Recoverable Damages for a Car Accident

Car accident lawyers play a crucial role in helping victims of car accidents seek compensation from insurance companies. They are skilled in determining liability, preserving evidence, and handling the claim process to ensure victims receive the compensation they deserve for their hardships.
Car accidents have a reputation for causing severe bodily injuries. According to the

, recent data show motor vehicle crashes resulted in over 2.8 million emergency department visits in a single year.

The types of compensation available in these cases may vary. Any financial, emotional, or physical losses you suffer in an accident through no fault of your own could be the basis of a successful personal injury lawsuit.
Past and Future Medical Expenses
Because of the severity of many car accident injuries, the cost of medical treatment following a crash can be substantial. Your injuries might have required you to:
Have surgery
Stay at the hospital
Take pain medications
Use assistive medical equipment
Get blood and imaging tests done
Schedule follow-up appointments with your doctor
Pain and Suffering

An unfortunate part of many car accidents is severe pain and suffering. Financial damages cannot erase the physical pain you have experienced, but they could provide you with some aid in dealing with this hardship. The scope of your pain and suffering compensation will largely mirror the extent of your medical bills.
Lost Wages

Property Damage

If your car was damaged or destroyed in the accident, you could hold the responsible party accountable for your losses. This compensation could include covering the cost of repairing or replacing your damaged vehicle.

items.question: What Kind of Video Footage Can Legally Be Used As Evidence?

children.text: Key Takeaways
Video evidence is admissible if relevant, authentic, and not unfairly prejudicial.
Authentication requires a witness to confirm footage accurately reflects events.
The chain of custody must show footage remained untampered from capture to court.
Footage may be excluded if irrelevant, unclear, unverified, or manipulated.
Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages in civil cases.

When an accident occurs, footage captured at the scene can affect the outcome of a personal injury or wrongful death case. Courts across New York increasingly rely on visual evidence to establish what happened, which is why understanding what types of recordings qualify matters from the beginning. Any footage obtained lawfully by an attorney may be used to support a claim, including cell phone footage, body camera footage,
security camera footage
traffic camera footage
, drone footage,
dashcam footage
, and footage captured by a camera crew.
A
Long Island personal injury lawyer
at
Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe – Long Island Personal Injury Lawyers
our
Long Island personal injury lawyer
team can evaluate the footage available in your claim and build a case around it.
Contact a Long Island Personal Injury Lawyer Near You
Free Consultation
What Types of Cases Benefit From Video Footage Evidence?
Video footage may be useful in personal injury cases involving:
A truck, bicycle, pedestrian, or
car accident
A slip or trip and fall
A medical error
An animal attack
A defective product
A workplace accident

In motorcycle accidents, video footage is of great importance, especially if you were using a GoPro or similar device at the time. GoPro footage provides a ground-level view of what happened. A skilled
motorcycle accident lawyer in Long Island

can build you a strong case based on the real-time video evidence you provide, as accident reconstruction, road conditions’ analysis, establishing liability, etc., become easier to accomplish. As long as it is reliable and relevant, the video footage motorcyclists provide can become highly persuasive evidence in a lawsuit.
Is Video Evidence Admissible in Court?
Many people ask:
Is video evidence admissible in court

after a serious accident in New York? And the answer is yes, video evidence is generally admissible in court provided it is relevant, authentic, and does not create unfair prejudice. The recording must connect directly to the facts of the case, provide an accurate depiction of the event, and be verified by witness testimony or chain-of-custody records showing the footage was never tampered with.
Courts typically allow video footage when these requirements are satisfied:
Authentication: A witness, such as a camera operator, bystander, or responding officer, must confirm the recording accurately reflects the events shown.
Relevance: The footage must make a disputed fact more or less likely to be true. According to the
New York Unified Court System
, relevant evidence is any material that makes a fact of consequence more or less probable than it would be without it.
Chain of Custody: A clear record must track who handled the footage from capture through courtroom presentation, ensuring no tampering occurred.
Originality: Unedited recordings are preferred, though authenticated copies may be accepted when reliability is intact.
Challenges arise when footage appears grainy, was captured unlawfully, or shows signs of alteration. Even unintentional edits can trigger admissibility disputes during litigation.
What Can Video Footage Show in Motor Vehicle Accident Cases?
Video footage can provide unparalleled detail in a motor vehicle accident case. Footage of a motor vehicle accident may show:
The collision between vehicles
The collision between a vehicle and a bicyclist or pedestrian
Specific illegal acts, like
running a red light
or stop sign, that caused the accident

Different types of video footage show different details. The camera angle, zoom level, and lens quality may determine how useful the video footage is. Dash camera and traffic camera footage may be especially useful in motor vehicle accident cases. These types of footage may have the clearest and most direct perspective of an accident.
What May Video Footage Show in Other Case Types?
Video footage may be available in lawsuits and insurance claims not involving motor vehicles. Videos may show:
A slip and fall accident, or the conditions that caused a slip and fall accident
A medical error occurring
A physical assault
An animal attack
A construction accident
A verbal admission of a product’s defect by a liable party
Our firm will seek any kind of video footage that can legally be used as evidence in your case.
What Type of Video Footage Is Prohibited?
Video footage may not be usable in a civil case if the video is:
Irrelevant to the case: Video footage must be pertinent to the case in question if it is to be used within your case.
Unclear: If the video footage is not clear, then it is difficult for either party to draw conclusions from the video.
Unverified: If video footage has unclear origins or either party cannot verify the video as authentic, then it may not be suitable as evidence.
Manipulated: Editing a video may spark allegations of manipulation, and this footage may not be usable as evidence.
Certain other conditions may make video evidence unusable in your case.
What If Video Footage Is Not Available or Usable?
If video footage is not available in your case, then your lawyer will make your case using other types of evidence. Your lawyer may prove a defendant’s fault by:
Obtaining witness accounts of your accident
Citing a police report that indicates the defendant’s fault
Reconstructing your accident with help from experts
Obtaining expert testimony
Taking photographs that indicate the defendant’s fault
Video footage may be unavailable in most cases. Though it is a valuable type of evidence, a video is not necessary to make your case.
What Is the Standard for Liability in Civil Cases?

Negligence is one standard for liability in wrongful death and personal injury cases. Our firm can use video footage and other evidence to prove a defendant’s negligence. Video footage may show the defendant acting in unreasonable and dangerous ways, and our team can use this video evidence as proof of negligence.
Our firm proves negligence by:
Establishing that the defendant owed you a duty of care
Proving the defendant’s breach of duty of care (perhaps using video footage)
Showing that the breach of duty of care caused your accident
We will then show the damages caused by a defendant’s negligence.
What Are Recoverable Damages in Civil Cases?

Recoverable damages in personal injury and wrongful death cases may include medical treatment, pain and suffering, lost income, lost financial support, diminished earning power, funeral expenses, and other damages.
A plaintiff’s recoverable losses may depend on:
Whether your case involves a death or only non-fatal injuries
How serious your injuries are
Whether you suffered a permanent disability
The cost of medical care and other economic damages
The severity of your pain and suffering
Our team seeks the compensation clients are entitled to under New York law.

items.question: What is the Car Accident Statute of Limitations in New York?

children.text: Traffic collisions happen in seconds, and the legal consequences begin just as fast. After a crash in New York, injured drivers and passengers face strict deadlines that can determine whether their claim succeeds or dies before reaching court. The
car accident statute of limitations in New York
typically gives victims three years from the date of the collision to file a
personal injury

lawsuit. However, this timeline can change in some situations, such as cases involving government vehicles, which require a notice of claim within just 90 days, while wrongful death claims, incidents involving minors, or situations with missing defendants follow different rules entirely, and once these deadlines pass, the right to pursue compensation is usually lost forever. Many people don’t realize how quickly these deadlines approach until they are already dealing with mounting medical bills and recovery challenges.
At
The Law Office Of Cohen & Jaffe – Long Island Personal Injury Lawyers
we understand how timing alone can change the entire outcome of a case, and we’re here to provide the guidance you need to protect your rights.
General Rule: File Your Car Accident Lawsuit on Time
Under
New York Civil Practice Law and Rules section 214
, a three-year statute of limitations applies to the majority of
personal injury lawsuits
that stem from car accidents. This timeframe begins on the day the collision occurs, not when treatment ends, or bills arrive.

This general rule applies to most car accident cases across Long Island, but it does not cover every situation. Some claims follow different timelines, which is why reviewing the facts early can help avoid preventable deadline issues.
Potential Compensation: You Can Recover Your Losses After a Car Accident in New York

Understanding filing deadlines also helps clarify what may be recovered in a car accident claim. A successful case may allow recovery for financial losses and personal injuries directly tied to the crash. Medical treatment, rehabilitation costs, and related expenses frequently form the foundation of these claims.
New York’s no-fault system covers basic economic losses up to a statutory limit, including necessary medical and hospital expenses, regardless of fault. According to
New York Insurance Law section 5102
, basic economic loss can reach up to $50,000 per person for covered medical and related costs, setting an initial baseline before a lawsuit becomes necessary.

When injuries exceed those thresholds or meet the serious injury standard, additional damages may be available. Pain and suffering, lasting limitations, and future care needs can all be considered, which is why the
car accident statute of limitations in New York
remains so important.
Steps to File a Car Accident Injury Lawsuit in New York

Filing a car accident injury lawsuit typically involves gathering medical records and crash evidence, preparing and filing the complaint in the proper New York court, and serving the at-fault party within the required timeframe. Each step must follow specific procedural rules, and missing the applicable deadline almost always results in dismissal, permanently preventing recovery of damages tied to the crash.
Key Exceptions & Special Circumstances
Some car accident claims do not follow the standard three-year timeline and require closer attention from the start. Common exceptions may include:

Government vehicles: When a city, county, or state vehicle is involved, a Notice of Claim must usually be filed within 90 days of the accident, followed by a lawsuit deadline of one year and 90 days from the date of the crash.
Wrongful death: These claims generally carry a two year filing period that begins on the date of death rather than the accident itself.
Minors: The filing deadline does not begin until the child turns 18, after which they have three years to file.
At-fault driver leaves New York: The statute of limitations may stop running while the defendant is outside the state.
These exceptions can shorten or alter the timeline, and the
car accident statute of limitations in New York
can vary depending on these details, which means each case must be reviewed on its own facts.

items.question: How Do I Dispute Car Accident Fault?

children.text: To dispute a car accident fault, you show an insurance company proof of the other party’s negligence, whether that be through a police report, witness statements, footage of the crash, or all three. Since New York is a no-fault state, you would be compensated for your damages even if you did cause the accident, but if you know you did not, you should dispute the decision if you are
deemed at fault

If the other driver caused the accident and you suffered serious injuries, you could file a personal injury lawsuit or liability claim against them to cover the costs that a no-fault insurance claim wouldn’t. At the
Law Office of Cohen & Jaffe – Long Island Personal Injury Lawyers
, we understand how crucial it is that the at-fault party is held responsible for their negligence.
Contact a Queens Car Accident Attorney Near You
Free Consultation
An Insurance Company Will Determine Fault for Your Claim

When you are involved in a car accident, the insurance companies of each driver will investigate the crash to determine how it occurred. This investigation will involve a statement from their insured driver, a review of the police report, and any other information the adjuster obtains. At the end of the investigation, the insurance company will decide who is at fault.
Insurance companies are not infallible, and some do not act in good faith. If a carrier finds that you were at fault when you know you weren’t, a
Long Island car accident lawyer
from our firm could help you dispute liability and pursue a fair resolution to your injury claim.

It is important to keep in mind that what the insurer decides is not a binding decision made in a court of law. Instead, it is an opinion issued by an adjuster for an insurance company. While this decision is not the final word on your injury claim, it will impact your potential financial compensation.
What Happens When the Insurance Company Finds You at Fault?

New York follows a no-fault insurance system, which means most accident-related medical expenses and lost wages are initially handled through no-fault coverage, regardless of who caused the collision. A determination of fault does not automatically prevent you from pursuing additional compensation. If you suffered a serious injury, you may still have legal options beyond no-fault benefits. An experienced personal injury attorney can evaluate the circumstances of the accident, determine whether you meet the serious injury threshold, and advise you on the appropriate legal steps to protect your rights.

The insurance company’s initial decision isn’t final, so being assigned fault doesn’t mean you’re out of options. You will get compensated regardless of fault, but you shouldn’t accept the blame. In addition, if you have serious injuries, you shouldn’t have to pay your own way for treatment when someone else caused them.

Disputing fault and pursuing a reasonable resolution to your insurance claim is your best option. A lawyer from our firm can handle communications with your insurance carrier and the other party. They can also file a lawsuit on your behalf if necessary. Litigating cases can be costly and time-consuming, so leave that to us. You have already dealt with enough.
Notifying the Carrier of Your Dispute Right Away is Crucial

If you disagree with the decision made by the insurance company in your case, it is important to notify the carrier of your dispute in writing. In some cases, notifying the carrier could push the adjuster to reconsider the decision.

Even if the carrier will not reconsider their decision by registering your objection, it could be possible to change their mind by providing additional evidence that backs up your case for liability. Your lawyer can handle all this for you.
Steps to Dispute Fault in a Car Accident
“Winning” an at-fault accident, or
how to win an
at-fault accident

under New York law, means successfully disputing an incorrect fault determination by presenting strong evidence to the insurance company or, when necessary, in court. To dispute fault after a car accident, you can follow these steps:
At the accident scene, if it is safe:
Do not admit fault: Express concern, but avoid statements that suggest legal responsibility.
Call the police: A police report creates an official record that insurers often rely on when determining fault.
Gather evidence: Take photos and videos of vehicle positions, damage, skid marks, traffic signs, and road conditions.
Exchange information: Collect contact and insurance details from all involved parties.
Identify witnesses: Independent bystanders can provide statements that help clarify how the crash occurred.
Document what happened: Write down what you remember as soon as possible while details are still fresh.

After the accident, seeking medical care is important even when injuries seem minor, since medical records help connect injuries to the crash. Reviewing the police report for errors also matters, as corrections or supplemental statements can clarify the facts. If an insurer assigns fault incorrectly, that decision can be disputed in writing with supporting evidence. In more complex cases involving disputed liability or damages, legal action may be considered to pursue additional evidence or court review.
The Outcome of the Police Investigation Could Impact Your Ability to Dispute Fault

The accident report issued by the police officer will play an outsized role in determining if you are found to be at fault or not. The insurance company is especially likely to determine that you were at fault if the police report reflects you caused the accident. This is also the case if you were ticketed for a moving violation at the time of the crash.

A traffic ticket or unfavorable police report could have a harmful impact on your insurance claim, but there are steps you could take to undo that damage. The police have been known to make mistakes, and there are ways to address these mistakes in the official records.

If the police report contains a factual mistake, it could be possible to request the officer to amend the report. If you wrongfully received a ticket for a moving violation related to the accident, fighting that charge could help your case. If you can avoid a conviction on your traffic ticket, you could improve your chances of successfully disputing fault.
Impact of Partial Fault on Compensation

New York follows a comparative fault system that allows injured parties to recover compensation even when they share some responsibility for the accident. However, the amount they receive is reduced proportionally to their assigned fault percentage. For example, if a driver is found 20 percent responsible, their total recovery decreases by that same amount.
Understanding
how to win an at-fault accident

dispute often means minimizing your assigned fault rather than eliminating it. Insurance companies frequently cite factors like speed, distraction, or poor road conditions to justify shared blame. Successfully challenging these conclusions requires strong evidence; witness statements, repair records, accident reconstruction reports, and consistent medical documentation help establish what actually happened.

Even a partial fault doesn’t eliminate your right to seek compensation for medical expenses, property damage, or ongoing treatment. The key is reducing the fault percentage assigned to you, as even small shifts can impact your final settlement.
Deadlines and Timelines for Disputing Fault
Timing shapes every fault dispute. According to the
New York State Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 605

, drivers involved in a crash must file a Report of Motor Vehicle Accident, Form MV-104, when injuries, death, or property damage over $1,000 occur. This report must be filed within ten days; failing to do so can complicate later disputes.
Under
New York Civil Practice Law and Rules Section 214

, there is a limited window of three years to bring a claim for property damage after a car accident. Once that deadline passes, courts can dismiss the case entirely, even when evidence clearly supports fault or damages. Knowing how much time is available helps injured drivers decide whether a dispute needs to move beyond the insurance process.
Disputing fault with an insurer should happen soon after a decision is issued. Delays can limit the ability to correct mistakes or gather supporting evidence.

, we know
how to win an at-fault accident

dispute by building strong cases that challenge unfair conclusions and reduce assigned blame. From gathering critical evidence to filing lawsuits against negligent drivers, we can handle every aspect of your claim while countering the tactics insurers use to minimize payouts.
